passage: Volcanologists distinguish eruptions less by their size than by their style. In an effusive eruption, low-viscosity magma—typically basalt, poor in dissolved gas and silica—rises and spills out as flowing lava, building the broad, gently sloping shields of volcanoes like those in Hawaii. In an explosive eruption, by contrast, the magma is rich in silica and dissolved gas; as it nears the surface and pressure drops, the gas comes out of solution so violently that it shatters the magma into ash and pumice, blasting it upward in towering columns. The same volcano can shift between these styles as the composition of its magma changes over time.
question: According to the text, what distinguishes the magma involved in an explosive eruption from the magma involved in an effusive eruption?

choices.text: It holds more dissolved gas and silica, so that escaping gas shatters it into ash and pumice near the surface.
It flows more readily across the surface, building the broad, gently sloping shields seen at volcanoes such as those in Hawaii.
It is poorer in silica and dissolved gas and rises slowly without fragmenting into ash.
It changes composition only after an eruption has already begun, rather than over longer spans of time.

explanation: Choice A is correct. The passage says that in an explosive eruption the magma is rich in silica and dissolved gas, and that as pressure drops near the surface the gas comes out of solution violently enough to shatter the magma into ash and pumice. Choice A reports exactly that contrast. Choices B and C describe the effusive case—free-flowing, gas-poor, shield-building magma—so they attribute the wrong properties to explosive eruptions. Choice D contradicts the passage, which says composition changes over time and can shift a volcano between styles, not only after an eruption starts.
